title: [Geomatics] Tree Species Classification in a Madagascar Tropical Dry Forest Using Multi-Temporal UAV Multispectral Imagery and Machine Learning
abstract: Accurate tree species mapping in tropical dry forests remains challenging because strong seasonal phenological variation and spectral overlap can limit discrimination from single-date imagery. This study evaluated the integration of wet- and dry-season unoccupied aerial vehicle (UAV) multispectral imagery, vegetation indices, Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) texture metrics, and digital surface model (DSM)-derived information for individual-tree classification in Kirindy Mitea National Park, Madagascar. UAV imagery at 11.3 cm ground sampling distance was linked to manually delineated crowns of 231 field-identified trees representing six canopy species. After missing-data filtering, 230 trees were retained and stratified into training (n = 186) and independent (n = 44) test datasets. Predictor selection was conducted exclusively on the training set: 68 candidate crown-level predictors were screened using Kruskal–Wallis tests with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction, followed by Spearman correlation filtering (ρ ≥0.80), yielding 34 predictors. Random Forest (RF) and radial Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers were tuned using the same repeated five-fold cross-validation framework (five repetitions), without synthetic oversampling. On the independent test set, RF achieved an overall accuracy of 65.9% (95% CI: 50.1–79.5%), Cohen’s kappa of 0.45, balanced accuracy of 0.65, Macro-F1 of 0.40, and MCC of 0.46. SVM achieved an overall accuracy of 59.1% (95% CI: 43.3–73.7%), kappa of 0.33, balanced accuracy of 0.64, Macro-F1 of 0.38, and MCC of 0.36. The paired difference in overall correctness was not significant (McNemar p = 0.606). RF permutation importance identified wet-season CTVI median, dry-season NDWI median, wet-season NIR contrast median, and wet-season KNDVI intra-crown variability among the highest-ranking predictors. These results show that multi-season spectral, textural, and DSM-derived information provides complementary information for tree-species discrimination, while class-specific performance and uncertainty indicate that broader validation and larger samples are required before operational transfer to other sites.

title: [Remote Sensing] Trajectory-SAM: Object Trajectory-Guided Segmentation for Remote Sensing Videos
abstract: The rapid proliferation of high-resolution remote sensing video (RSV) has made object segmentation an increasingly critical yet challenging task. Existing methods face two fundamental limitations in this domain: (1) the intrinsic complexity of RSVs arising from diminutive object sizes, dense distributions, and drastic scale variations; (2) prohibitive computational overhead and latency caused by the massive spatial resolution of remote sensing imagery. To address these challenges, we propose Trajectory-SAM, a novel object trajectory-guided segmentation framework tailored for rapid and accurate object segmentation in RSVs. Specifically, we first employ a Graph Neural Network to extract representative keyframes, improving data utilization efficiency while suppressing attention drift and interpretation bias induced by redundant frames. We then introduce Temporal-LoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy for the Segment Anything Model (SAM), substantially enhancing its spatiotemporal contextual understanding in remote sensing domains. Finally, we devise a sample-augmentation-based knowledge distillation strategy to accelerate inference without sacrificing segmentation quality. Extensive experiments on the SAT-MTB, iSAID, and VHR-10 datasets demonstrate that our proposed Trajectory-SAM achieves superior performance, establishing a compelling trade-off between accuracy and speed.

title: [Remote Sensing] Optical Multispectral Indices Versus Microwave-Based Soil Water Index for Surface Soil Moisture Assessment: A Linear Mixed-Effects Analysis of Pixel-Level Heterogeneity over a Tuscan Agricultural Landscape
abstract: Soil moisture (SM) assessment underpins applications ranging from climatological studies to land management and emergency response. Microwave techniques already support operational SM products, but at a spatial resolution limited to 1 km. Optical multispectral indices have been proposed as a complementary source of information at finer resolutions (10–100 m), yet vegetation heterogeneity has generally been handled by masking or stratifying the land cover rather than by modeling its effect. Here, we compare three indices (the Normalized Difference Infrared Index, NDII; the Normalized Multi-band Drought Index, NMDI; and the Visible and Shortwave Infrared Drought Index, VSDI) over a heterogeneous agricultural area near Grosseto, Tuscany, using 31 Landsat-8 OLI images acquired over four summers. Evaluated against the Copernicus Soil Water Index (SWI), VSDI performed best both when averaged over the test area and when analyzed at the pixel level (1 km) and was therefore selected for further analysis. A linear mixed-effects model with pixel-dependent intercepts resolves a within-pixel VSDI–SWI repeated measures correlation of 0.714, against 0.411 for the pooled regression. Allowing the slope to vary as well shows that vegetation density governs both the baseline level of VSDI and its sensitivity to soil moisture, with the within-pixel correlation falling from 0.84 on bare soil to 0.30 under a dense canopy.

title: [Remote Sensing] Unraveling Spatial Associations of Surface Subsidence in Typical Oil Production Areas of Songyuan City by Integrating Time-Series InSAR and Deep Learning
abstract: Oilfield subsidence threatens infrastructure and sustainable development. Although facility detection, factor-association analysis, and deformation forecasting have each advanced considerably, their systematic integration remains insufficiently explored for oilfields in agricultural plains, where C-band SAR decorrelation over cropland and wetland yields sparse and uneven deformation observations. This constraint complicates facility extraction, quantitative analysis of associations among interacting factors, and robust temporal prediction. To address these challenges, this study develops and applies an integrated modular workflow for the monitoring, analysis and prediction of surface subsidence in a typical oil production area of Songyuan City, China. We first used PS-InSAR for high-precision deformation monitoring and validated the results with leveling survey data. Subsequently, the YOLOv12 model was utilized for automated oil well identification, and the Geodetector model was applied to quantify the spatial associations between subsidence and the examined natural and anthropogenic factors. Finally, a hybrid LSTM–Transformer model was developed for time-series prediction and applied to forecast deformation through November 2025, twelve months beyond the final SAR acquisition. Results indicate significant spatial differentiation in deformation, with a maximum subsidence rate of −26.0 mm/y. Analysis identifies oil well density and surface elevation as the leading spatial factors among those examined, and the buffer zone analysis indicates a distance-related association of approximately 700 m between oil wells and subsidence rates. The hybrid model demonstrated superior overall accuracy compared to standalone LSTM and Transformer models. The findings provide concrete scientific support for risk mitigation in oil cities.

title: [Remote Sensing] DSFormer: An Enhanced Dual-Selective Fusion Transformer Framework for Hyperspectral Image Classification++
abstract: Hyperspectral image classification requires joint modeling of spectral signatures and spatial structure. In patch-based classification, each input patch is assigned the label of its center pixel, although neighboring pixels may belong to different land-cover classes. This setting motivates coordinating shallow spatial features, contextual refinement within the patch, and supervision of the resulting representation. We propose DSFormer++, an enhanced framework based on the original Dual Selective Fusion Transformer Network (DSFormer). Shallow Feature Compensation (SFC) combines shallow and patch-embedded features through gated residual fusion before the backbone. The Collaborative Global–Local (CGL) module applies an additional refinement operation with shared parameters before token selection at two backbone stages. Pixel Contrastive Loss (PCL) uses center-pixel labels to supervise projected patch embeddings during training. The proposed method achieves overall accuracies of 96.50%, 97.60%, 95.35%, and 94.83% on the Pavia University, Houston13, Indian Pines, and WHU-HH datasets, respectively. Component comparisons and approximately parameter-matched controls characterize configuration-dependent effects. Numerical checks assess consistency between the stated operations and their implementation, and an additional Botswana experiment extends the evaluation to a satellite wetland and woodland scene.

title: [Remote Sensing] Explainable Transformer-Based Estimation of Surface NO2 Concentrations Across Fujian Province Using TROPOMI Observations
abstract: Atmospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is one of the major pollutants affecting environmental quality and human health, yet accurate surface NO2 (NO2Surface) estimation remains challenging due to complex nonlinear relationships between satellite-derived NO2 column density (NO2column) and near-surface concentrations. Here, we proposed an explainable transformer-based framework for daily NO2Surface estimation across Fujian Province, integrating Sentinel-5P TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) NO2 observations with meteorological data, digital elevation model (DEM), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), nighttime light (NTL), and population density (PD). Using ground-based observations, Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) was trained and benchmarked against five conventional machine learning (ML) algorithms. Under random five-fold cross-validation, TabPFN achieved the highest accuracy, yielding a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.93, root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.56 μg m−3, mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.05 μg m−3, and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 5.82%, with R2 improvements of 0.17–0.26 and RMSE reductions of 45.3–53.5% relative to CatBoost and RF, respectively. Additional station-grouped spatial validation and independent temporal validation yielded R2 values of 0.86 and 0.79, respectively. The reconstructed NO2Surface distributions revealed a clear coastal-to-inland gradient, with concentrations frequently exceeding 50 μg m−3 in urbanized coastal areas but generally below 15 μg m−3 in northwestern mountainous regions. Strong seasonality was evident, with the peak NO2Surface and widespread pollution in winter, contrasting with lower and more localized levels in summer. Temporal analyses revealed persistent declines in NO2Surface, with annual mean concentrations decreasing by 11.7% from 2019 to 2020 and a further decline of 1.6% in 2021, while descriptive daily slopes were approximately −0.003 μg m−3 day−1. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis highlighted TROPOMI NO2column and BLH-corrected NO2 (NO2BLH) as the most influential predictors, accounting for 15.07% and 11.36% of the contribution, respectively, with temperature- and humidity-related variables exhibiting strong nonlinear responses. This study provides an accurate and interpretable framework for 1 km gridded NO2Surface estimation and characterizes the predictive relationships associated with regional NO2 variability.

title: [Remote Sensing] A Hierarchical Framework for Arctic Shoreline Type Mapping Using SAR and Optical Satellite Imagery
abstract: Although intertidal-zone delineation and shoreline or coastal geomorphological classification have been extensively investigated, relatively few studies have integrated these complementary information layers within a unified and operational remote-sensing framework for oil-spill emergency response. With increasing development and marine transportation activities in the Arctic, detailed and spatially explicit shoreline information is essential for oil-spill response planning and coastal hazard assessment along the Canadian Arctic coast. A key challenge is to reliably characterize the spatial extent and geomorphological variability of Arctic intertidal shorelines under substantial temporal variability in tidal inundation and environmental conditions. This study presents a hierarchical shoreline classification framework designed to support oil-spill emergency preparedness and response planning. The framework integrates Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) backscatter, temporal-change and structural descriptors, and Sentinel-2 water-sensitive indices to derive a composite shore-zone proxy that captures spatial and temporal information on tidal inundation and coastal surface characteristics. This proxy supports Level 1 shore-zone mapping, while high-resolution optical imagery enables subsequent Level 2 shoreline-type classification. The framework was evaluated in four Canadian Arctic coastal areas representing diverse coastal landscapes and environmental conditions, including differences in tidal regimes, water turbidity, floating ice, and geomorphology. Results indicated that mapping accuracy remains constrained for tidal zones and substrates smaller than or comparable to the sensor’s spatial resolution. For Level 1 shore-zone mapping, unsupervised classification of the temporal and composite indices achieved overall mapping accuracies of 56–73% for the Upper Shore Zone across three study areas. For Level 2 shoreline-type mapping, Random Forest classification of high-resolution satellite imagery, including WorldView and GeoEye imagery, achieved overall accuracies of 81–85% across the four study areas. These results demonstrate the potential of the composite shore-zone proxy to integrate complementary SAR and optical information for consistent characterization of Arctic shore zones, while the subsequent shoreline-type classification provides additional geomorphological detail. Together, the hierarchical products provide spatially explicit shoreline information that can support the identification and prioritization of shoreline areas for oil-spill response planning and resource allocation.

title: [Remote Sensing] A Transformer Network for Settlement Generalization Integrating Raster Maps and Remote Sensing Images
abstract: To address the challenges of reliance on manual expertise and insufficient automation and intelligence in settlement generalization during scale transformation, this paper proposes a multi-scale settlement generalization model (DSG-Trans) based on the fusion of dual-source data: raster maps and remote sensing images. Leveraging the cartographic correspondence between remote sensing image resolution and map scale, this model integrates source-scale maps with specific low-resolution remote sensing imagery to automatically generate target-scale raster maps that adhere to cartographic specifications. The model employs a bidirectional cross-attention mechanism and a Transformer architecture to facilitate the semantic integration of dual-source data, while a progressive upsampling strategy is utilized to reconstruct spatial details. Additionally, a composite loss function incorporating four constraints is designed to enhance the quality of settlement generalization. Experiments were conducted in New York City, USA, using a multi-source dataset constructed from 3D-GloBFP building footprint data and multi-source remote sensing imagery, focusing on two scale transformation scenarios: 1:5000 to 1:10,000 and 1:5000 to 1:25,000. The results indicate that the proposed method effectively learns and simulates expert generalization knowledge, significantly improving the automation level and scale adaptability of map generalization while preserving geometric morphology and spatial distribution patterns.

title: [Remote Sensing] 3DMAUNet: A 3D Memory-Augmented Deep Unfolding Network with Dynamic Momentum Updating for Snapshot Compressive Spectral Imaging
abstract: Coded aperture snapshot spectral compressive imaging (CASSI) enables the recovery of hyperspectral images (HSIs) from a single two-dimensional compressive measurement, serving as a core paradigm in modern computational imaging. However, HSI reconstruction from under-sampled measurements is a severely ill-posed inverse problem. Existing deep unfolding methods typically treat each iterative stage independently and model spatial–spectral features in a decoupled manner, which neglects intrinsic spatial–spectral coupling and lacks persistent cross-stage information propagation. To tackle these issues, we propose a deep dynamic 3D memory-augmented unfolding network (3DMAUNet) for HSI reconstruction. Based on the momentum-accelerated generalized alternating projection framework, 3DMAUNet retains the strict mathematical interpretability of iterative optimization while integrating data-driven learnable components. Specifically, we design two key modules: (1) a 3D memory-augmented learning module equipped with a persistent memory bank, which explicitly encodes cross-layer spatial–spectral correlations to enable efficient inter-stage information transfer and long-range dependency modeling; and (2) a learnable dynamic fast momentum updating module, which fuses cross-stage spatial–spectral attention features to estimate task-adaptive momentum coefficients, accelerating convergence and enhancing the robustness of feature updating. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world HSI datasets demonstrate that 3DMAUNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative reconstruction performance.

title: [Forests] Phosphorus Addition Enhances Ecosystem Multifunctionality While Reshaping Multi-Trophic Biodiversity–Function Relationships in a Tropical Cloud Forest
abstract: Background: Phosphorus (P) availability regulates tropical forest functioning, yet how P enrichment reshapes biodiversity–ecosystem multifunctionality (EMF) relationships remains poorly understood, especially in tropical cloud forests (TCFs), where rising nutrient inputs may shift the balance between ecosystem productivity and biodiversity conservation. We investigated how contrasting P availability alters multi-trophic biodiversity and its relationships with EMF. Methods: Using a three-year field P addition experiment in a TCF at Bawangling, Hainan Island, China, we examined the effects of Control, Low P, and High P treatments on multi-trophic biodiversity. We quantified above- and below-ground biodiversity components and assessed EMF using seven ecosystem functions governing productivity and elemental turnover. Results: P addition increased soil nutrient availability and enhanced EMF, but simultaneously reorganized biodiversity structure by promoting plant functional and bacterial diversity while reducing phylogenetic and fungal diversity. Importantly, P availability shifted the biodiversity dimensions associated with ecosystem functioning: phylogenetic diversity was the dominant biodiversity dimension associated with EMF under ambient P limitation, whereas plant and root functional diversity showed stronger associations with EMF under moderate P addition. Under high P availability, biodiversity–EMF relationships weakened, suggesting a potential decoupling between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning under excessive nutrient supply. P addition was associated with changes in EMF, soil nutrient status, and multi-trophic biodiversity. Our findings suggest that P enrichment may simultaneously enhance EMF and alter the biodiversity–EMF relationships associated with ecosystem functioning. Incorporating P dynamics into ecological monitoring frameworks may therefore improve understanding of tropical forest responses to future nutrient enrichment.

title: [Forests] Fungal Communities and Their Environmental Correlates in BSCs Under Sand-Fixing Plantations in Alpine Sandy Land
abstract: The fungal communities within biological soil crusts (BSCs) of alpine sandy lands remain poorly understood, particularly regarding their associations with long-term plantation restoration. Four types of sand-fixing plantations (Salix psammophila, Salix cheilophila, Caragana korshinskii, and Populus simonii) in the Gonghe Basin were chosen as study sites, and bare sand, algae crust, and moss crust samples were obtained from each plot. Soil physicochemical properties and extracellular enzyme activities were measured, and the fungal community was characterized by Illumina high-throughput sequencing of the ITS1 region. We systematically examined how key predicted guilds of fungal communities and their environmental factors changed across crust types, and characterized the differentiation of predicted guilds. Our main results are summarized below: (1) Ascomycota and Basidiomycota dominated at the phylum level, while Preussia, Alternaria, Paraphoma, and Endocarpon dominated at the genus level. (2) Moss crust had the highest fungal richness and evenness, followed by algae crust, whereas bare sand had the lowest values. Furthermore, PCoA-ANOSIM further revealed marked differences in BSC fungal community structure among the plantations. (3) Spearman’s correlation analysis, CCA, and the Mantel test indicated that the plantations were associated with fungal community differentiation through variation in edaphic physicochemical properties and extracellular enzymatic activity. Furthermore, pH, AK, and AP were associated with fungal community composition in both crust types, with ALP and SUC additionally important in algae and moss crusts, respectively. (4) FUNGuild predictions indicated that Undefined Saprotroph was the dominant predicted guild and that saprotrophy was the dominant trophic mode in the BSC fungal communities of the study area. This study revealed the fungal community composition and organization of BSCs across various crust types, and identified the factors associated with these communities in different artificial sand-fixing plantations in alpine sandy land. These findings may offer a microbiological foundation for restoring alpine sandy land ecosystems in the future.
